other_side: Zitron would say the Fable 5.1 launch proves his point rather than Anthropic's. In the Manifesto he argues that everyone talks about price as if price were the problem, when the real problem is the number of tokens burned — and Artificial Analysis finding 5.1 seventy per cent hungrier and dearer per task than its predecessor is exactly the pattern he describes, where the 'cost of intelligence' falls on paper while the cost of actually getting something done rises. He notes the earlier Fable model plateaued at around eleven per cent of Anthropic's usage because of its price, that labs are incentivised to build inefficient models, and that subscriptions are subsidised precisely because ordinary users would not pay the true cost. So the 'personal model architecture' NLW recommends is, on Zitron's reading, users being asked to do unpaid cost-engineering for a product whose pricing and rate limits can change at the vendor's whim.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is the real cost of a completed task, not the sticker price per million tokens. Both accept as fact that Fable 5.1 burns far more tokens than Fable 5, that Artificial Analysis measured a higher cost per task despite cheaper cache reads, and that users are hitting rate limits fast. The empirical question that will resolve is whether cost per finished job falls once defaults are fixed and norms settle, or keeps rising with each generation; the observable is Artificial Analysis-style cost-per-task figures over the next few months, alongside whether Anthropic's usage limits loosen or tighten. The pure worldview residue is whether tokens are a fair price for capability or a subsidy trap. NLW is vindicated if the sub-agent fix and effort-level tuning bring measured cost per task below Fable 5's, and if enterprises keep paying. Zitron is vindicated if each new model costs more per job and subscriptions are withdrawn in favour of metered billing. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is that both now expect subscriptions to end and API pricing to arrive. Watch the next independent cost-per-task benchmark.
